choices: Gloves only
Gloves and a surgical mask
Gloves and a HEPA respirator mask
A gown and a surgical mask, but no gloves
questions.explanation: Tuberculosis spreads through the air, so standard precautions with this patient mean gloves plus a HEPA respirator mask, not just a surgical mask.
questions.question: You and your partner are called to a sick person who is coughing and reports fever, night sweats, and a history of tuberculosis. Your partner walks in and starts assessing the patient with no gloves and no mask. Before he gets any closer, what should he put on?

choices: Through a bite from an infected insect
Through contaminated food he ate
By touching a contaminated surface and then his face
Through the air he breathed
questions.explanation: TB is carried on airborne particles the patient coughs out, so infection from this patient would be airborne transmission.
questions.question: Your partner skipped his precautions with that same coughing tuberculosis patient. If he ends up infected with the patient's illness, how did the disease most likely reach him?

choices: Report the exposure to the infection control officer
Nothing — the chance of infection from one call is too small to bother with
Ask the hospital staff to isolate the patient
Just make sure the equipment gets sanitized before the next call
questions.explanation: Any possible exposure gets reported to the agency's infection control officer so it can be documented and followed up.
questions.question: After the call, your partner realizes he assessed a patient with a history of tuberculosis without any protective equipment. What should he do about the possible exposure?

choices: Because the hospital will refuse to accept the patient
Because he could become infected and pass an airborne disease on to coworkers, other patients, and his own family
Because a single exposure automatically ends his certification
Because the patient could sue him personally
questions.explanation: An airborne exposure doesn't stop with him. If he becomes infected, he can spread the disease to coworkers, future patients, and his family.
questions.question: Your partner shrugs off having skipped precautions with the coughing tuberculosis patient, saying the only person he put at risk was himself. Why is that wrong?

choices: An acute stress reaction
Posttraumatic stress disorder
A cumulative stress reaction
A delayed stress reaction
questions.explanation: His signs built up gradually over weeks of repeated stress rather than erupting after one single incident — that pattern is a cumulative stress reaction.
questions.question: Over the past several weeks, with call volume up and almost no downtime between calls, your partner has changed. He's disinterested in the work, shows up late, takes unnecessary risks, and sits alone at the station instead of socializing with the rest of the crew. What is he most likely experiencing?

choices: Headaches
Taking unnecessary risks
Night sweats
Withdrawing from coworkers
questions.explanation: Headaches, risk taking, and isolation are all recognized signs of stress. Night sweats were the patient's tuberculosis symptom, not a stress sign.
questions.question: You're reviewing the warning signs of stress so you can keep an eye on your partner. Which of the following is NOT usually a sign of stress?

choices: You've started enjoying your hobbies again
Your concentration at work has noticeably sharpened
You feel more patient and decisive than before the incident
You've lost interest in your normal activities and find yourself irritable, snapping at people over small things
questions.explanation: Loss of interest in normal activities, irritability, and frustration are classic signs of poorly handled stress, alongside the sleep, appetite, and fatigue changes already described.
questions.question: Six months into the job, you work a mass-casualty incident involving a bus full of schoolchildren, some of them severely injured. Weeks later a coworker says you don't seem like yourself, and you realize your sleep is off, your appetite is gone, and you're tired all the time. Which additional change would fit the same pattern of stress that isn't being handled well?

choices: Unwind with a few drinks after each shift
Put in for a vacation and not think about it until then
Ask the supervisor to just give him time off
Get into regular physical activity away from the workplace
questions.explanation: Regular physical activity away from work is a proven stress reducer. Alcohol makes stress worse, and time off alone doesn't build a coping habit.
questions.question: You want to help your partner start managing his stress before it gets worse. Which suggestion is most likely to actually help?

choices: Improve your diet and sleep, and build a social life and interests outside of work
Drink more caffeine so you stay alert through long shifts
Volunteer for extra shifts so you stay too busy to think about it
Keep your feelings to yourself so coworkers don't worry
questions.explanation: Better diet and sleep, changing stress-producing habits, and having a social network and interests outside work are all proven stress reducers. Extra caffeine and bottled-up feelings work the other way.
questions.question: After the bus incident, you're working with a counselor and exercising regularly, and it's helping. Which other change is a proven way to keep stress from wearing you down over the long haul?

choices: His morning runs
His habit of drinking to unwind after every shift
Eating regular, balanced meals
Keeping a consistent sleep schedule
questions.explanation: Alcohol is not a recommended way to manage stress — it disrupts sleep and adds to the problem. Exercise, proper diet, and sleep are the recommended tools.
questions.question: Your partner lists his habits for you: morning runs, regular balanced meals, a steady sleep schedule, and a few drinks after every shift to unwind. Which of his habits is NOT a recommended way to manage stress?

choices: Give it more time — these reactions always pass on their own
Double your caffeine intake so you can get through shifts
Meet with a mental health counselor or an employee assistance program consultant
Ask to work only the busiest shifts so you get used to it
questions.explanation: When self-help techniques like exercise, relaxation, and talking it out aren't enough, the next step is professional help from a mental health counselor or an employee assistance consultant.
questions.question: Weeks after the mass-casualty call, you've been exercising, using breathing and relaxation techniques, and talking with a supportive friend, but you're still not sleeping, still have no appetite, and still feel exhausted. What's the advisable next step?

choices: Changes in appetite, stomach and bowel problems, backache, headaches, and fatigue
Fever, night sweats, and a cough that won't quit
Sudden one-sided weakness and slurred speech
A racing heart that starts and stops without warning
questions.explanation: The long-term physical effects of stress include changes in appetite, gastrointestinal problems, backache, headaches, and fatigue. Fever and night sweats point to infection, not stress.
questions.question: Stress that drags on for months takes a physical toll on a responder. Which set of complaints fits the long-term physical effects of stress?

choices: Backache, headaches, and stomach problems
Fever, chills, and night sweats
Calm focus and a sharper memory
Fear, depression, guilt, oversensitivity, anger, and irritability
questions.explanation: Long-term psychological effects of stress include fear, depression, guilt, oversensitivity, anger, irritability, frustration, and dull or nonresponsive behavior. Backache and headaches are physical effects.
questions.question: That same long-running stress affects responders psychologically, too. Which set of reactions fits the long-term psychological effects of stress?

choices: He becomes too set in his ways to learn new protocols
His patients get less-efficient care, and the wear on his body and mind can shorten his career
His coworkers will simply pick up the slack with no downside
Nothing — stress only affects life off duty
questions.explanation: Poorly managed stress weakens the body, and the depression and anxiety that come with it erode concentration and focus. Patients get poorer care, and the responder's health and career can be cut short.
questions.question: A responder lets his stress go unmanaged for a long time. On calls he starts losing concentration and his focus slips. What's the most direct danger this creates?

choices: Guilt and fear of medical personnel, along with past experiences with illness or injury
The color of the ambulance
The day of the week the call happens
How long the crew has been on shift
questions.explanation: Reactions are influenced by things like age, socioeconomic background, chronic disease, substance use, past experiences with illness or injury, and feelings such as guilt or fear of medical personnel — not by the call's logistics.
questions.question: You treat two patients with similar injuries on the same shift. One family is calm and cooperative; the other is angry and agitated. Which factor can shape how a patient or family reacts to the stress of an illness or injury?

choices: A routine transfer of a stable patient to a nursing home
Standby at a school football game where nobody needs treatment
A multiple-patient incident with critically injured children and overpowering sights, smells, and sounds
A single patient with a sprained ankle who is calm and cooperative
questions.explanation: Stress runs highest on dangerous, high-demand calls: multiple patients, critically ill or dying patients, and overwhelming sights, smells, and sounds.
questions.question: Now that you've learned to spot stress in yourself and your crew, which call should you expect to hit you and your coworkers the hardest?
